text:
maya: Quick heads-up, infra alerted on a host-side CPU uplift (~+12%) after yesterday's kernel-selection rollout. Traces point at a spike in syscalls around writev/http2 framing and UTF8 normalize in the tokenization path. :eyes:

sam: Can you paste the pprof/top samples?

maya: Sure — grabbed a short perf run. Command: `perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 60` then `pprof -symbolize=none host_bin perf.data`. Top samples snippet:
```
writev                          27.8%
parse::tokenize::normalize_utf8 14.9%
http2::hpack::encode            10.4%
socket::flush_small_writes       9.6%
kv_cache::lookup                 6.1%
```
Notably `writev` and a tiny socket flush helper are very hot.

taylor: Huh. Any change in frame size distribution after the kernel change? If we're flushing at smaller batch sizes that'll kill syscalls.

maya: Exactly — compared current vs baseline framing histograms. Current: ~70% frames <1k (spike at 256-512). Baseline: ~25% small frames, more 4k+ frames. Suspect batching heuristic + kernel minibatch decision -> more frequent flushes.

leo: That would make sense. Kernel pickup changed minibatch cut thresholds; fewer tokens per minibatch -> more round trips to host. We should instrument the batching window and flush incentives.

sam: Repro steps? Can we run a local synthetic that forces the new kernel choices and measures write sizes?

maya: I pushed a small reproducer script to my branch that simulates request mix: many short prompts + streaming. It reproduces the small-write-heavy pattern locally.

ci-bot: CI canary results for `maya/smallwrite-coalesce` are available: https://ci.redwood/redwood/canaries/1234 (passed unit + e2e, smoke shows host CPU + network syscall drop on canary).

ops-bot: Metrics from prod-dedicated1 canary run (first 30m): host p99 latency +7% initially, CPU down after patch.

taylor: Proposed quick mitigation: coalesce small writes on the host proxy for up to 2ms or until buffer reaches 1KB. Pseudocode:
```c++
// coalesce small writes to reduce writev/syscall pressure
if (to_write.size() < 1024 && now - last_write_ts < 2ms) {
  buffered.append(to_write);
} else {
  flush(buffered + to_write);
  last_write_ts = now;
}
```
We add a metric for coalesce_count and avg_coalesced_bytes.

sam: Looks good. Also add an opt-out flag per route and a telemetry gating so we don't regress streaming tail behavior.

leo: I'll run kernel-selection A/B toggles to see if we can nudge kernel back while we evaluate. If kernel is the root cause we should revert or adjust thresholds.

maya: I'll open PR with the coalesce change + telemetry and a small unit test to ensure no long stalls. Branch: `maya/coalesce-smallwrites`.

sam: I'll own the canary rollout. Plan: canary 5% on prod-dedicated1 for 30m, track host CPU, syscall rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, and framing histogram.

ci-bot: Canary job created: job/4582. Collector dashboards: link -> https://dashboard.redwood/host/writev-coalesce/4582

(30m later)

maya: Canary update: p50 latency stable, host CPU decreased ~9% vs pre-patch, syscall rate for writev down ~30%, small frame fraction fell from 70% -> 35%. No error increase. :thumbsup:

taylor: Nice. Any change in model output quality / streaming semantics?

maya: No functional diffs in our smoke evals. Streaming saw slightly higher per-message batching (expected) but end-to-end time for tiny prompts improved on average.

leo: Kernel AB test shows the kernel selection tweak accounts for most of the minibatch shrinkage. We'll follow up with a kernel threshold adjustment to reduce tiny minibatches long-term.

sam: Next steps: merge coalesce change behind a kill-switch flag (off by default), ship telemetry, follow-up kernel patch ticket assigned to leo/taylor. I'll close the canary and prepare rollout notes.

maya: TL;DR: regression caused by kernel-driven minibatch shrink -> host small writes and syscall pressure. Short-term host-side coalescing reduces syscall pressure and CPU. Mid-term fix: adjust kernel selection heuristics + add batching tolerance.

leo: Filed follow-up: ENG-PRF-2678 (kernel threshold tuning).

sam: Great work everyone. Kudos for quick triage. :clap:
